stages.title: Advanced grammar
stages.hook: "He wore", "he dressed someone" and "he got dressed" all come from the root ל־ב־ש. What changes the meaning?
explain: Hebrew has seven verb patterns, the binyanim: pa'al (simple), nif'al (often passive or reflexive), pi'el (intensive or causative), pu'al (passive of pi'el), hif'il (causative), huf'al (passive of hif'il) and hitpa'el (reflexive). The root stays the same and the pattern changes the meaning.

Example with ל־ב־ש: lavash (he wore), hilbish (he dressed someone, hif'il), hitlabesh (he got dressed, hitpa'el). With ל־מ־ד: lamad (he studied), limed (he taught, pi'el). With ס־ג־ר: sagar (he closed), nisgar (it closed or was closed, nif'al).

Each binyan has its own pattern of vowels and prefixes in the past, present and future. A dictionary lists verbs in the 3rd person masculine singular past form, so knowing the binyan lets you predict the other forms.
stages.mnemonic: Same root, new costume: seven costumes, seven ways to act.
sentences: The teacher taught the students a lesson.
I got dressed quickly in the morning.
The window was closed by the wind.

o: Pa'al (simple), since it has no prefix
gq.why: The hit- prefix marks hitpa'el, which is often reflexive.

gq.q: What does pi'el limed (taught) add to pa'al lamad (studied)?
o: A causative idea: making someone learn
A passive idea: something is done to the subject
gq.why: Pi'el is often causative or intensive.

panel.q: A learner sees "nisgar" and "sagar". What is the likely difference?
o: Nisgar is the nif'al: it was closed or closed itself
Nisgar is a noun meaning a door or a lock
panel.why: Nif'al often expresses passive or reflexive meaning.

panel.q: Why must you know the binyan to form the future?
o: Each binyan has its own prefix and vowel pattern
Future is the same for all
The future is the same for all binyanim
panel.why: Patterns differ between binyanim.

panel.q: Explain how root and binyan work together in Hebrew verbs.
panel.model: The root gives the core idea and the binyan gives a pattern that adds a meaning such as active, passive, reflexive or causative.
panel.why: Root plus pattern gives predictable meanings.

teach.model: Hebrew verbs are built on a root and one of seven patterns called binyanim. The pattern adds meanings such as simple, causative, passive or reflexive.

stages.title: Complex sentence patterns
stages.hook: "The door of the house" in Hebrew is "delet ha-bayit": two nouns side by side, with no word for "of". Which noun gets "the"?
explain: The construct state, smikhut, joins two nouns: delet ha-bayit, "the door of the house". The first noun (nismakh) changes form and never takes ha-; the second noun (somekh) can take ha-. If the second noun is definite, the whole phrase is definite.

Changes in the first noun: a feminine singular -a becomes -at (mora → morat ha-kita, the class teacher f.). A masculine plural -im becomes -ei (talmidim → talmidei ha-kita, the students of the class). Some nouns change their vowels, such as bayit → beit (beit sefer, school).

Besides smikhut, Hebrew can use shel: ha-delet shel ha-bayit. Conditions use im (real) and ilu or lu (unreal): ilu haya li zman, hayiti ba, "if I had time, I would come". The spoken language often uses shel more than smikhut.
stages.mnemonic: Smikhut: the first noun leans on the second, so it loses its "the".
sentences: The students of the class went on a trip.
The door of the house is open.
If I had time, I would come.

gq.q: Which is correct for "the school" in smikhut?
gq.why: Only the second noun takes ha-.

gq.q: What happens to a feminine ending -a in the first noun of smikhut?

panel.q: Why is "talmidei ha-kita" not "talmidim ha-kita"?
o: The plural ending -im becomes -ei in the first noun
The second noun is feminine, so the plural changes
panel.why: Masculine plural -im changes to -ei in the construct.

panel.q: Why is "delet ha-bayit" definite?
o: The second noun has ha-, and this makes the whole phrase definite
The first noun has ha-, so the whole phrase is definite
panel.why: Definiteness of the construct is decided by the last noun.

panel.q: Explain the difference between "delet ha-bayit" and "ha-delet shel ha-bayit".
panel.model: Both mean the door of the house. The first uses the construct state (smikhut) and is common in writing; the second uses shel and is common in speech.
panel.why: Hebrew has two ways to express possession.

teach.model: Smikhut joins two nouns. The first noun changes form and never takes ha-. The second noun can take ha-, and this makes the whole phrase definite.

points.ask: Which noun does not take ha-?
Is there another way to say of?

stages.title: Extended conversations
stages.hook: You are invited to an Israeli home for Friday night dinner. What would you say when you arrive and when you leave?
explain: Hospitality is important in Israeli culture. A host may say bruchim ha-ba'im (welcome, plural), titkabed (help yourself) and tirgash ba-bayit (make yourself at home). A guest says toda al ha-irukh (thanks for the hospitality) and often brings a small gift, such as flowers or something sweet.

For an invitation: esmakh le-hazmin otkha le-aruchat erev be-yom shishi, "I would be glad to invite you to dinner on Friday". To apologise: ani mitnatsel al ha-ikhur (I apologise for being late). Notice that formal verbs often have the same form, but men and women must still use different forms: ani mitnatsel (m.), ani mitnatselet (f.).

Israelis are often direct and informal, using first names even with older people. The tone may seem blunt to visitors but is usually friendly. A tradition for Shabbat dinner may include a blessing over wine and challah; guests may join in or watch respectfully.
items: I would be glad to invite you
what do you do for a living? (to a man)
can you help me? (to a man)
sentences: I would love to invite you to dinner on Friday.
Please come in and make yourself at home.

gq.q: What does "titkabed" invite a guest to do?
o: Help themselves to food or drink
Leave the house after finishing the meal

gq.q: How does a woman say "I apologise"?
gq.why: The present tense has a feminine form with -et.

panel.q: Why might an Israeli host seem very direct?
o: Informality and directness are common social styles, not rudeness
They are angry with the guests and want them to leave
panel.why: Style differs by culture and context.

panel.q: Which phrase best thanks a host?
panel.why: It thanks for the hospitality.

panel.q: Why do men and women use different forms in conversation, for example "ani mitnatsel" and "ani mitnatselet"?
panel.model: In the present tense Hebrew verbs agree with the gender of the speaker or subject, so a woman uses the feminine form.
panel.why: Present-tense verbs have gender forms.

teach.model: Hosts say bruchim ha-ba'im and titkabed. Guests thank them with toda al ha-irukh. Use esmakh le-hazmin to invite politely. Verbs show the speaker's gender.

stages.title: Formal and informal registers
stages.hook: You write to a university and to a close friend. Which Hebrew would change most: the words, the grammar or the tone?
explain: Hebrew registers range from formal written language to casual speech and slang. Letters and official texts use set phrases: la-khavod (to), adoni ha-nikhbad (Dear Sir), ani poneh elekha be-inyan (I am writing to you regarding) and be-khavod rav (respectfully). The formal register uses complete sentences and polite fixed phrases.

Spoken Hebrew uses contractions and slang: ba li (I feel like), yalla (let's go, from Arabic), nu (come on, from Yiddish), davka (actually, specifically). Slang changes fast and differs by age and group, so use it only when you are sure.

The Academy of the Hebrew Language recommends standard forms and creates new words. Speakers often use the common forms in speech and the standard forms in writing and news. Using the right register shows respect and fits the situation.
stages.mnemonic: Formal opens with a ribbon; informal with a wave.
sentences: Dear Sir, I am writing to you regarding the course.
I would like to schedule a meeting.

gq.q: Which phrase would you use to close a formal letter?
Where does the slang word "yalla" come from?

panel.q: Why would "ba li" be out of place in a formal request?
o: It is colloquial; formal Hebrew uses ani rotze or avakesh
It is rude in all settings
It is rude in all settings, even among friends
panel.why: Register should fit the situation.

panel.q: What is the role of the Academy of the Hebrew Language?
o: It sets standards and coins new words
It prints newspapers and sets their style
panel.why: It recommends standard forms and creates terms.

panel.q: Explain why a speaker should adjust their Hebrew between writing to an official and speaking to a friend.
panel.model: Official writing uses formal, standard phrases that show respect. Speaking to friends allows informal and slang forms, which would sound inappropriate in a formal letter.
panel.why: Register shows respect and fit.

teach.model: Formal letters use phrases like adoni ha-nikhbad and be-khavod rav. Everyday speech uses slang such as yalla and nu. Choose the register to fit the person and situation.

points.ask: What do people say in speech?

stages.title: Reading articles and literature
stages.hook: A newspaper headline is short and often leaves out words. What is left when you take away "the", "is" and "was"?
explain: Reading Hebrew ranges from news to poetry. Newspaper headlines are short and use present-tense or passive forms: ha-roman turgam le-safot rabot, "the novel was translated into many languages" (pu'al: turgam). Common newspaper words: iton (newspaper), katava (article), koteret (headline).

Hebrew poetry has a long history. Modern poets include Haim Nahman Bialik, Rachel, Leah Goldberg and Yehuda Amichai, who writes in plain, everyday words. S. Y. Agnon won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1966. A poem (shir) has stanzas (batim; one bayit is a stanza or a house) and often uses imagery.

When you read, identify the genre first: news gives facts; a poem is dense and figurative. Use your knowledge of roots to guess new words, but check context. Unpointed text means you must supply the vowels yourself.
stages.mnemonic: Bayit means house: a stanza is a little house for words.
sentences: The newspaper published the article yesterday.
The poet writes about love and homeland.
The novel was translated into many languages.

gq.q: Which Hebrew writer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1966?
gq.why: Agnon shared the 1966 Nobel Prize in Literature.

gq.q: What does "bayit" mean in a poem?
o: A rhyme at the end of a line
gq.why: Bayit (house) is also a stanza or verse.

panel.q: Why is "turgam" a passive?
o: It is pu'al/huf'al: the doer is not named
It has the suffix -im, which always marks a passive
panel.why: Passive binyanim show the action done to the subject.

panel.q: Why must a reader of unpointed Hebrew supply the vowels?
o: Short vowels are usually not written
Hebrew has no vowels at all, only consonants
panel.why: Context tells which vowels are meant.

panel.q: Name one difference between reading news and reading a poem.
panel.model: News is direct and gives facts; a poem is dense and figurative, using images and rhythm.
panel.why: Genre changes how we read.

teach.model: Newspapers use short headlines and passive forms. Poems have stanzas called batim and use imagery. Agnon won the Nobel Prize in 1966.

points.ask: What is special about news Hebrew?

stages.title: Essay and correspondence writing
stages.hook: You write an email to a university in Hebrew. How do you open and close it politely?
explain: A formal email has a subject (nose), a greeting, the purpose, details, a request and a closing. Phrases: ani kotev elekhem be-nogea le- (I am writing to you regarding), metsuraf (attached), ashmakh lekabel et teshuvatkhem (I would be glad to receive your reply), be-vrakha (with regards).

An essay has an introduction (mavo), body paragraphs (psikot) and a conclusion (sikum). Keep gender agreement and verb tense consistent. When you write to a group or to an unknown person, use plural forms or neutral phrases, because Hebrew verbs and pronouns show gender.
Hebrew email uses the same punctuation as English. Remember that parentheses and quotation marks are mirrored by the right-to-left direction, and that numbers are written left to right.
stages.mnemonic: Letter: Hello, Purpose, Details, Request, Goodbye.
sentences: I am writing to you regarding the scholarship.
The document is attached to this message.
I would be glad to receive your reply.

gq.q: Which word means "attached" in an email?
Why use a plural address like "elekhem" to a committee?
o: It addresses several people and avoids gender choice

panel.q: Why is gender agreement tricky in a formal email to a stranger?
o: You may not know their gender, so plural or neutral phrases help
panel.why: Verbs and pronouns mark gender.

panel.q: A student's essay has no conclusion. What should be added?
o: A sikum summarising the main ideas
A new topic that was not mentioned before
panel.why: An essay needs a summarising conclusion.

panel.q: List the main parts of a formal Hebrew email.
panel.model: Greeting, subject and purpose, details, request, and a polite closing.
panel.why: Formal emails follow a conventional order.

teach.model: A formal email has a greeting, a subject, details, a request and a closing. An essay has an introduction, paragraphs and a conclusion. Keep gender agreement.

points.ask: How do I give the purpose?

stages.title: Translation fundamentals
stages.hook: Hebrew has no word for "is" and uses different words for "you" to a man and a woman. How can a translator move that into English?
explain: Translating is not swapping words. In Hebrew the present "is" is often missing: ha-bayit gadol (the house big). A translator adds "is" for English. The other way, English "I have" must become yesh li ("there is to me") and "you" must become atah (m.) or at (f.), or a plural form.

New words are created by the Academy of the Hebrew Language and by speakers. Makhshev (computer) comes from the root kh-sh-v ("to think, to calculate"). Many technical words are borrowed: telefon, internet, universita. Hebrew words often have both a borrowed and a coined form, and speakers may choose.

A good translator reads the whole text, finds the meaning, then writes natural English. Literal translation can hide meaning (for example idioms); free translation can lose details. Check key words, tone and register.
sentences: The translator reads the text carefully.
Translation is more than replacing words.
I use the dictionary every day.

gq.q: How is "I have a car" said in Hebrew?
gq.why: Hebrew says "there is to me a car".

gq.q: What problem arises when translating English "you" into Hebrew?
o: Hebrew needs to choose atah (m.), at (f.) or plural
Hebrew has no word for you

panel.q: The Hebrew sentence "ha-yom kar" has no verb. How should it be translated?
panel.why: English needs the verb "is".

panel.q: Why is a literal translation of "kol ha-kavod" ("all the honour") a risk?
o: It is an idiom meaning well done
It has no meaning in any other context
panel.why: Idioms need meaning-based translation.

panel.q: Why does a translator need to think about register as well as meaning?
panel.model: The same idea can be formal or informal; a good translation keeps the tone and suits the audience.
panel.why: Meaning includes style and tone.

teach.model: Translating means carrying meaning, not words. Hebrew omits is in the present and has gendered you. A translator adds is, reorders and checks tone.

points.ask: What should a translator carry across?

stages.title: Regional varieties and cultural context
stages.hook: Hebrew was spoken in the Bible, written for centuries and spoken again in daily life only since about 1900. How can a language return like that?
explain: Hebrew has a unique history. Biblical Hebrew was spoken in ancient times; later it was used mainly in prayer, law, poetry and letters, while Jews spoke other languages such as Yiddish, Ladino and Judeo-Arabic. Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and others promoted its use as a spoken language from the late 19th century, and it became an official language of Israel.

Modern (Israeli) Hebrew has absorbed words from Yiddish (nu), Arabic (yalla, sababa), English and Russian. Pronunciation traditions differ: some communities, such as Yemenite Jews, preserve older distinctions like ע and ח; most Israelis today merge these sounds. Arabic has a special status in Israel and is the first language of its Arab citizens.

Immigrants (olim) from many countries have shaped Hebrew, and slang spreads quickly through media. Name the community or tradition when you talk about pronunciation, and avoid saying one accent is "better".
stages.mnemonic: An old language, woken up and welcomed into the kitchen.
sentences: Hebrew was revived as a spoken language.
Many Hebrew words come from Arabic and Yiddish.
Immigrants brought new languages to the country.

gq.q: Who is most associated with reviving Hebrew as a spoken language?
gq.why: Ben-Yehuda campaigned for daily use of Hebrew.

gq.q: Which language is a Jewish language of Spanish origin?
gq.why: Ladino developed from medieval Spanish; Yiddish from German.

panel.q: Why is it correct to say Hebrew was "revived" rather than "invented"?
o: It was used in writing and prayer throughout history and became spoken again
It was a dialect of Arabic
panel.why: It existed as a written and liturgical language.

panel.q: Why do Yemenite traditions matter to linguists?
o: They are wrong, because they differ from most Israelis
panel.why: They help reconstruct historical pronunciation.

panel.q: Name two languages that have influenced Modern Hebrew and give an example word.
panel.model: Arabic gave words like yalla and sababa; Yiddish gave words like nu.
panel.why: Hebrew absorbed words from the languages of its speakers.

teach.model: Hebrew was written and prayed in for centuries and revived as a spoken language in the 19th and 20th centuries. Modern Hebrew has words from Yiddish, Arabic and other languages.

points.ask: How did it become spoken again?

stages.title: Structured debates and presentations
stages.hook: In a debate you must give an opinion, a reason and an example. Which Hebrew words can start each one?
explain: A structured argument uses signposts: li-da'ati (in my opinion), ki (because), te'on (argument), re'aya (evidence), mi-tsad sheni (on the other hand), ani rotze lehosif (I would like to add), ani kholek al (I disagree with). Rebut respectfully: ani lo maskim, ki...

A short presentation in Hebrew has a greeting, a topic statement, three points with examples, and a thank-you: toda al ha-hakshava (thank you for listening). Speak clearly, stress the last syllable of most words, and keep your verbs in agreement with the gender of the subject.

Jewish tradition values debate: the phrase makhloket le-shem shamayim ("a dispute for the sake of heaven") describes a disagreement that seeks truth, not victory. Whatever your culture, a respectful debate listens first, answers the argument and not the person.
stages.mnemonic: Opinion, reason, example, answer: four steps up a ladder.
sentences: In my opinion, reading is more useful than television.
On the other hand, technology saves time.
I would like to add one point.

gq.q: Which phrase introduces your own view?
Which phrase signals a contrasting point?
gq.why: It means on the other hand.

panel.q: A debater says "re'aya" after a claim. What is expected next?
o: An insult aimed at the other debater
panel.why: Re'aya means evidence.

panel.q: Which is the most respectful way to disagree?
o: ani lo maskim, ki ... (I disagree, because ...)
ata to'e (you are wrong) with no reason
panel.why: Giving a reason keeps disagreement respectful.

panel.q: Describe a simple structure for a short debate speech.
panel.model: State your opinion, give reasons and evidence with an example, answer the other side, and finish with a conclusion.
panel.why: Clear structure persuades.

teach.model: State your opinion with li-da'ati, give a reason with ki, add evidence and an example. Use mi-tsad sheni for the other side and end with a conclusion.

points.ask: How do I give an opinion?
How do I answer and finish?
